What a $249 listing video actually costs to make

Updated 25 August 2026 · 5 min

We charge $249 for a listing film. The AI render inside it costs about $4.41.

That is not a confession. It is the most useful thing we can tell you about this category, because once you know it, every price you are quoted starts making sense — including the ones that are far too high and the ones that are suspiciously low.

The actual bill

A 42-second film at 1080p, on the model we use, bills at a flat rate per second of finished video. There is no volume discount, no batching trick, and the price does not change whether the second is of a kitchen or a driveway.
Runtime 42 seconds
Render $4.41
Card processing $7.52
Total direct cost $11.93

Ninety-five per cent of what you pay is not the render.

So what is it?

Three things, and they are the whole business.

Judgement about the order. Photographs arrive as a folder. A film needs a sequence — a buyer's walk, not a file listing. Which room opens, which room closes, where the camera goes outside and comes back in. Get it wrong and you have a slideshow with motion.

Refusing the shots that will not work. A rear-facing patio shot cut to a front-framed aerial produces a film that looks like a different house, because there is no path a camera could fly between them. We check for that before rendering and tell you, which occasionally means telling a paying customer that their photo set needs one more picture.

The disclosure pack. An on-screen mark, a hosted page carrying your unaltered originals, a QR code, and caption text. That page is the artefact California's §10140.8 requires a link to, and building it properly is most of the reason this is a business rather than a script.

Why the market prices are what they are

A traditional listing video runs several hundred dollars, and a drone package not much less, because somebody drives to the property. That is a real cost and those prices are honest. What they buy is a person with a camera and an afternoon.

We are not cheaper because we found a cheaper way to do that. We are cheaper because we do not do it at all — we start from photographs that already exist. It is a different product that happens to sit in the same slot on an invoice.

What this tells you about a suspiciously cheap quote

If somebody quotes you thirty dollars for AI listing video, the render is not what they are saving on. At these costs nobody is saving meaningfully on the render.

They are saving on the judgement and the disclosure pack — which is to say, they are shipping you the file and keeping none of the liability. That is a real thirty-dollar product. It is just not the same product, and the difference shows up when a buyer asks why the back of the house looks like that.

And about an expensive one

Equally: a four-figure quote for AI video from your own photos is charging you agency rates for a process that has no crew, no travel and no shoot day. Ask what the extra thousand buys. There may be a good answer — a real editor, a custom cut per platform, a strategist who knows your market. There may not be.

The number we would rather you took away

$4.41. Not because it makes us look good — it arguably does the opposite — but because it is the number that lets you evaluate every quote you get, including ours.

If someone cannot tell you roughly what their render costs, they either do not know or would rather you did not. Neither is a good sign in a vendor you are trusting with the disclosure on a live listing.

This is not legal advice — it is what a vendor's costs look like from the inside. The statute referred to above is California Business and Professions Code §10140.8, added by AB 723; read it at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.

Figures are from our own cost model at the time of writing and move with provider pricing. The render rate is verified against the provider's own pricing tool; card processing is the standard 2.9% plus thirty cents. Operator time is not included above — it is real, it is the largest remaining input, and it is what the rest of the price pays for.

We make drone-style video from photographs an agent already has, and every delivery carries the disclosure pack described above — because we had to build it for ourselves first. How it works.
